What is a deathpool?

You pick 10 celebrities that you think will die before the end of the year. Points are given based on a number of different things, such as the age of the celebrity when they died and the manner in which they died. You are essentially betting on loss of human life.

You should research before you make your picks. Try to find someone who looks like they could die, rather than someone you wish would die. For example, betting on an 80 year old with pancreatic cancer is probably a far safer pick than betting on a healthy 50 year old, though you would get more points for the 50 year old (see below).

What are the rules?

Points are given as follows: 1 point = every year under 100 the pick is when they die. For example, Fidel Castro is 90 this year, so you will receive 10 points if you pick him and he dies.

You are only allowed ONE PICK that is involved in open conflict, such as an ISIS leader. There will be a -50% points deduction for these picks.

You can not murder, or be involved in the murder of any of your picks. This will result in disqualification.

Choosing picks that are on death row is disallowed.

The game will end at midnight on New Year's Eve. The winner will be the person with the most points when the clock strikes 12.

How do I start playing?

Submit your username and 10 picks here. Message a mod to confirm that you did send a form, this way we can ensure that people aren't submitting forms as other users. After you have submitted a form, your name will be entered on the leaderboard with your score. The leaderboard will be updated when a celebrity dies. In the event that one of your picks dies, please alert a mod so they can update your score, as we might miss the deaths of some picks.

Bonus Points

25 Points

  • The Amy Winehouse - Your pick dies from an overdose. Toxicology report must be made public before midnight on New Year's Eve for points to be added.

  • The Kurt Cobain - Pick commits suicide.

  • The Whitney Houston - Your black pick dies in February (Black History Month).

  • First Blood - You are the first person to get a dead pick. This is only applicable if nobody else had the same pick.

50 Points

  • The John Lennon - Your pick is murdered. Again, murdering or having anything to do with the murder of your pick will result in immediate disqualification.

  • The Machine Gun Kelly - Your pick dies on their birthday.

100 Points

  • Last Call - Your pick dies on December 31st.

It is much, much more likely that this is, at worst, blowback from the attempts to control mosquito populations. It could be that the species targeted to reduce the incidence of Dengue fever (which has been markedly successful, I should note) has left an ecological niche to be filled by another similar species that is more hospitable to Zika. If true, this is unbelievably unfortunate, but not something that really could have been predicted. Zika just wasn't on the radar at the time. More likely still is that the two events are not directly connected at all, and this outbreak would actually be worse if it were not for the successful reduction of mosquito populations. Remember that this region of Brazil played host to the 2014 World Cup, and will also be hosting the 2016 Olympics. This means an enormous increase in the flow of people who would otherwise not have a reason to visit, particularly from Africa.

It also appears that the genetic modifications to the mosquitoes are considerably less effective if tetracycline is present in the environment. Guess what one of the leading antibiotics used on livestock is? Tetracycline. 75% of the drug passes in the urine of the animals without being metabolized. That was foreseeable, and failure to account for it was short-sighted, but it doesn't seem to have completely rendered the program ineffective, only less effective.

Releasing male insects that are either sterile or that produce nonviable offspring is actually a well-known and long used technique, and it typically works -- sometimes enough to dramatically reduce insect populations long term, other times serving only to suppress them temporarily. Inserting the "fix" into the genes of the animal directly is a bit of a new twist, though hardly an unexpected one now that CRISPR is cheap and ubiquitous.

After working for a regulatory body, the vast majority of what they do feels restrictive and petty until you consider the possible consequences.

ALL VALVES MUST BE DOUBLE-CHECKED BEFORE AN OPERATOR LEAVES THEM UNATTENDED. FLOW METERS ARE MANDATORY FOR TANKS OVER 5,000GAL.

As an example: something as simple as "all valves must be double-checked and confirmed shut before left unattended" sounds like a nobrainer, right? A waste of regulatory time and energy. Until a chemical plant operator leaves the valve to a 15,000-gallon tank of iprOH partly open and overnight this drains the entire thing into the municipal sewer. The next morning, our wastewater operators wake up to a total-kill of their plant's microbes, something that takes about 2 weeks to recover from. We can't shut down the sewer system, and our entire standby capacity is 6 hours of normal waste flow - so that means we're going to basically be dumping sewage (filtered and settled, but still fecal-positive and untreated) into the river for ~2 weeks while we get the plant back online.

All because some dumbass didn't fully shut a valve.

Does something like "make sure all valves are shut" sound petty? It does, but only in the context of a homeowner for whom the most critical valves they own might be to the water main and gas lines. When a valve has the potential to dump thousands of gallons into public systems, then it's fair to ask for some regulatory influence.

Usually this boils down to band-aids at the municipal level, simple things like "Prove you have a way to safely clean up this stuff if it spills" and "Make sure your employees are using best practices and aren't cutting corners" in response to issues that have either come up or have been brought up in regional discussion.

I'll absolutely agree that demanding SCPP and best practices from a startup can be a barrier to entry, but it's a pretty significant part of businesses' operation costs as well. Plants will happily install 2,000,000-gallon storage tanks just so they have the ability to divert and store waste flow, on the off chance that something goes wrong they have someplace to put the mistake until they know how to clean it up safely.

REGULATORY BODIES CAN INSPECT YOU WHENEVER THEY LIKE AND FOR ANY REASON

And we also have the other side of things happening as well: there are compounds in the blue water of port-a-johns that kills bacteria, called quaternary amines or just Triple Quats. These are bio-accumulative, meaning they can kill a bacterium, then when the microbe dies it's released to kill again. Can you imagine why we don't want that in a wastewater treatment plant? Yeah. The plant can handle a small amount of it, but only in a trickle dosage. For this reason we charge port-a-john companies high rates and make them dump their blue waste into a special holding tank that we feed at its own rate.

Well, after looking at plant data for a while we started to notice semi-regular drops in performance. What on earth could be causing this? We checked our industrial sources, nobody was dumping anything harmful (they usually call beforehand to give us warning) and yet we kept finding rapid spikes of some toxin in our system. This was harming plant performance enough that we were violating DNR discharge limits on a regular basis.

Turns out, a nearby port-a-john company had decided our rates were unreasonably high and decided to take their pumper trucks to one of our pipe junctions and dump straight into the sewer system! They just opened the manhole and ran a hose, drained their whole truck in the middle of the night and drove away again. They saved their company about $25,000 every time they did this and thought they were being so clever. Police caught them red-handed once we determined with manhole was being used, and we negotiated the $holyshit in penalties down because it would have sunk the business. Instead they were put on probation and we wrote a section into our municipal code that says we're allowed to inspect anyone, anytime, no questions asked. Also, our main pipe junction boxes now have padlocks on them. (There were also some vandalism issues with dumbass kids who thought it was funny to drop rocks and hear the SPLOOSH)

I can completely understand the arguments against regulation when it comes to things like stupid plumbing codes, but at the industrial level there are some very good reasons for regulation - the bigger the possible mistake, the more layers of protection society should demand against it.
